In that year, this responsibility was transferred to the newly formed immigrant integration division and integrated with its multi-ethnic activities section. At the same time, related documentation functions were transferred to the research and documentation division. Hence there has not been an ethnic press section in the citizenship branch since 1966.
By the creation of this new division and its multi-ethnic-activities section, the branch increased its ability to keep informed about the needs of ethnic groups and to meet those needs.

Perhaps I should point out to the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac and to the committee that it is the opinion of the Chair that the amendment moved by the hon. member is irrevelant to subclause 2 (c) in that it introduces different methods of reception while the clause deals only with broadcasting in the sense to which the Broadcasting Act applies.
Second, it appears to the Chair that the phrase "by any means whatsoever" might well be interpreted as including methods of broadcasting not covered by this clause, or even by the bill or the act itself.
Third, it also seems to the Chair that the amendment is redundant with respect to subclause (e) of clause 2.
It is for these reasons and with regret that I must rule the amendment moved by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac out of order. Shall clause 2 (c) carry?

Mr. Chairman, I had not expected the amendment to be ruled out of order. However, the objection of the Chair that the introduction of new means of broadcasting is too wide perhaps fits in with the suggestion that I was going to make to the hon. member who moved the amendment, namely that the purpose of the amendment, as I see it, is to reassure the people of Canada, and to emphasize in the Broadcasting Act itself, that while it is necessary to regulate broadcasting and even to bring distribution systems under the Broadcasting Act, we in this house are very cognizant of the right of individual citizens to hear and see the programs that are available.
I was going to suggest to the hon. member that he delete the phrase "by any means whatsoever" from his amendment. I think this would have the effect of meeting the
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting objection that the Chair found to the introduction of extraneous matter. The objection of the Chair that this is already covered in subclause (e) would not apply, and there would then simply be added to the freedom of expression enunciated in subclause (c) the declaration of freedom to receive the broadcast programs that are available.
I would point out that this clause is already subject to the general regulations made under the act. If my suggestion were adopted there would simply be added to the right to freedom of expression, the right to freedom to receive.
I suggest that here we are coming up tight against what is a fundamental concern to a great many Canadians in this country. I think we should consider that concern at this point, and I suggest this type of amendment provides a good vehicle to decide whether or not the government should be in the position to impose a kind of censorship on the programs people may see or hear.
It has been said by many that we can buy magazines from the United States and read what we like, that we can listen to the radio broadcasts from Moscow or somewhere else, and so on. Even though some attempts are made to jam certain programs, nevertheless anyone who has the necessary equipment can listen to any radio program he wants.
I suggest the same sort of reasoning applies to television sets. If the signal is in the airwaves and people can receive it, then they should be permitted to do so. In this connection it is cogently argued that, situated as we are close to the United States, the citizens of Canada are able to receive and enjoy powerful transmissions which emanate from that country. On the other hand, some parts of Canada farther away from the United States are not reached by these transmissions and the people in those areas are unable to view the programs.
It is also argued that by regulating cable networks we are discriminating against certain Canadians. In effect we are preventing one segment of the population from receiving programs they might like to receive whereas another segment-the largest segment of the population-has perfect freedom in this regard.
Certainly the question whether or not there is any attempt to inhibit people in their choice of program must be approached most carefully. I think generally speaking all members of the house would agree that there is no
5916	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting such thing as protecting people from propaganda, or trying to see they are not seduced by one or other kind of propaganda from foreign parts. Therefore any resort to an artificial means of controlling what may be seen and heard is so undesirable that the subject hardly need be discussed in the house.
One difficulty which arises here is this. The parliament of Canada controls the taxpayers' money, many millions of which is used for the purpose of advancing and protecting Canadianism-Canadian culture. Therefore, if we do not have some means to control broadcasting there is a distinct possibility that regulations made so loosely as to permit by any means whatsoever the distribution of United States programs could completely nullify the efforts of parliament in this regard. We do not want to spend the taxpayers' money for nothing, Mr. Chairman. Neither do we want to see parliament or the regulatory body passing regulations which would prevent people from using equipment that is available to receive programming. Nevertheless electronic equipment is available which could completely defeat what we are trying to do.
I am not sure that we are yet in a position to foresee what will happen when the whole of Canada is covered by satellite t.v. transmissions and there is no need for cablevision or for booster stations. The only way the people could be prevented from receiving these transmissions would be to try to jam the satellite broadcasts. I do not think anyone would argue with the proposition that it should be within the legislative ambit of the parliament of Canada to control the airwaves above this country and to regulate what may enter them. But it is a different matter when we ask whether we want to regulate what enters our airwaves; and if there is some proclivity in this direction it will be difficult to decide how we do this and to what extent.
I think that what is necessary at the moment is to put into the act simply a reminder that while the arguments for regulation are many, and while there is some concern about using in the best possible way money spent by the C.B.C. on the preservation of Canadianism, there is an overriding concern for the right of every citizen of this country to hear and see whatever programs he or she wishes.
When I put it in that way, Mr. Chairman, I have not forgotten that there does exist in our criminal legislation provisions in connection with certain types of seditious propaganda. For example we can regulate certain

DEBATES	January 24, 1968
kinds of questionable programs on the airwaves. Nevertheless, regulation of cablevision or other broadcasting systems should be for the primary purpose of preserving Canadian sovereignty over the means of communication in this country and to maintain an orderly use of airwaves and channels. In addition, its purpose should be the broadening of the possibilities of Canadians to see what can be seen in the best way possible and for the least money possible. Also, we should bear in mind that the money we are spending should have some effect in promoting Canadianism.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Though Your Honour has just ruled one amendment out of order I wish to move another amendment which is almost identical to it except that my amendment would leave out certain words that the Chair considered objectionable. The amendment I propose would add between the words "expression" and "subject" in line 19 thereof the following; "and the right of Canadians to receive all broadcasting programs available to them." That amendment would apply to subclause (c). The clause as amended would then read:
(c) all persons licensed to carry on broadcasting undertakings have a responsibility for the public effects of the programs they broadcast but the right to freedom of expression and the right of Canadians to receive all broadcasting programs available to them, subject only to generally applicable statutes and regulations, is unquestioned;
May I move that amendment, Mr. Chairman? I apologize to the minister for my lack of courtesy in not having advised her of the amendment. Yesterday I thought it would be some time before we would reach this clause and I was caught unprepared. The minister is entitled to notice of the amendment and I regret that I did not give her that notice.

May I ask my hon. friend to stand this matter? Obviously he is reading from the wrong copy of the bill. His amended clause contains the words "public effects". Bill C-163, as reported back by the committee, did not contain that wording. If my hon. friend would stand his amendment perhaps he might refer to the new reprint of the bill and deal with the matter then. I have no objection to standing this matter for the time being.
I thank the minister. May I ask the committee to give me time to consider?

Agreed.
January 24, 1968

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The committee will proceed with discussion of subclause 2(d) and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer.
Mr. Chairman, before we proceed with the next clause I wish to say that I am somewhat confused by the statement concerning the revised version of the bill. I presume that some hon. members have it.
We all have it. There has been a new printing.
Well, I do not have a copy. It is not in my file of bills. I should like to obtain a new copy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The committee will now proceed to clause 2(d). The hon. member for Red Deer moved an amendment to subclause (d). His amendment sought to insert after the words "public controversy" in line 5 of the bill the following:
"while ensuring that the most broadly held opinions receive appropriate consideration";
His amendment also sought to add, after the words "other resources", the words:
"while alert and responsive to public preferences in this and other aspects of programming".
Clause 2(d) would then read as follows:
"The programming provided by the Canadian Broadcasting system should be varied and comprehensive and should provide reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy, while ensuring that the most broadly held opinions receive appropriate consideration, and the programming provided by each broadcaster should be of high standard, using predominantly Canadian creative and other resources, while alert and responsive to public preferences in this and other aspects of programming".

Mr. Chairman, I shall not repeat my remarks of last night. The purpose of the amendment is to strengthen the bill and it is intended to do nothing else. The amendment seeks to make it clear to management that they have a responsibility for program content. I believe it is just as necessary for this bill to provide management with guide lines for carrying out its responsibilities with respect to programming content as with respect to the technical side of broadcasting. These remarks apply to both the C.B.C. and the private sectors of broadcasting. I commend this amendment to the minister and to the committee. I trust that the amendment is acceptable and that members of the committee will support it.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Miss LaMarsh: I regret that I cannot lend my support to the amendment. I am sympathetic toward the hon. member's intentions. We all hope what he hopes with respect to program content. I think that any manager worth his salt would feel that it is his responsibility to broadcast conflicting views on matters of public controversy. He would broadcast those views particularly that are reflected by large segments of the public. Nevertheless, I am afraid that what the hon. member seeks to do by way of amendment cannot be legislated.
During the committee proceedings members of my hon. friend's group came forward with amendments which in themselves were unobjectionable. Various amendments dealt with matters such as good taste. The wording of such amendments, or the spirit of such amendments, would be acceptable to anyone. But that spirit cannot appear in a piece of legislation.
I do not think that anyone should be required to decide, as a matter of statute law, what a broadly held opinion is. Those who are in this chamber or in public life know that broadly held opinions in this country may vary almost daily or almost hourly. To ask some individual to determine what a broadly held opinion is, is to place on that individual an unsupportable burden.
To require broadcasters to remain alert and responsive to public preference "in this and other aspects of programming" is placing great difficulties in their way. Though that wording may seem innocuous, it imposes a frightening stricture on those whom it may affect. For instance, they may be left open to charges that they are not alert and not responsive to public preferences. Public preferences change from time to time and they change sharply, as we all know. Though I may agree with my hon. friend's sentiment I cannot, on behalf of the government, agree to enshrine it in legislation. I must therefore inform my hon. friend, reluctantly, that I am not prepared to accept the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I support the essence and theme of the amendment that the hon. member for Red Deer has moved. In common with the hon. lady I admit that I am not satisfied with the precise wording of the amendment.
On December 21 I served notice to the minister and the committee when I was speaking in the general debate and taking an umbrella approach to the legislation that I intended to
January 24, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting move an amendment to subclause 2(d). I shall move amendments at subsequent stages of the bill dealing with other matters.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I find that in essence the approach taken by the hon. member for Red Deer has presaged my own. He has moved an amendment which I intend to support, but should that amendment fail to pass I shall move an amendment of my own which is worded somewhat differently but which is also calculated to provide the degree of responsibility and objectivity in the national broadcasting service that he and I, together with a good many other Canadians, desire and feel has been lacking in the public affairs sector of the C.B.C., particularly in television, in recent months if not in recent years. I cannot accept the position the minister takes with respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer. With all due respect I submit that no undue restriction would be placed on management by the acceptance of an amendment worded in the form put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer. Nor would undue restriction be caused by an amendment such as I intend to advance should the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer fail.
I believe Canadians have a right to expect of those in positions of authority in both public and private broadcasting that a high degree of responsibility implying conscientiousness in terms of objectivity of presentation will be striven for, achieved and maintained. This does not impose an undue restriction upon our broadcasters. In fact, it would constitute an important guide line which should in any case be provided for administrators in what, after all, is a relatively new industry, a relatively new profession. I for my part would be satisfied with an amendment which simply suggested that programming be planned and devised in such a way as to guarantee responsible and balanced treatment of subjects of public controversy. As I say, the wording I favour differs from that adopted by the hon. member for Red Deer. However, we share the same view as to the need for responsibility in broadcasting, a view which has been advanced by other members of the committee including, for example, the hon. member for Elgin and the hon. member for Leeds, during the debates which have taken place in this chamber in recent months.
We share the view that some set of guide lines in connection with objectivity in public


affairs broadcasting in this country is overdue. We share a measure of concern about the one-sided partisan approach which has been taken all too often in public affairs broadcasting, particularly by C.B.C. television. A great many Canadians are similarly concerned. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer is intended, as is my own, to be fair both to broadcasters and to the listening public. All it is intended to do is to place the onus for ensuring balanced presentation upon the management and operators of individual stations-I use the word "operators" not in a technical but in a literary sense. The intention is to place the onus upon these people to maintain a posture of concern with regard to program schedules in public affairs programming, for instance, an attitude which would ensure that where one viewpoint is presented to a substantial extent over a period of time an opportunity will then not only be provided but will be guaranteed for other points of view to be expressed.
This does not constitute a rigid stricture imposed on the management of radio or television stations. All management has to do is keep an eye on the programming schedule or else delegate others to do so, to "vet" the program schedule as a responsible authority in a profession which we all hope is rapidly becoming a responsible one. The least one can ask is that management maintain vigilance over the programming schedule and meet their responsibilities as persons in a position to shape public opinion and attitudes in Canada toward controversial issues of the day, making sure that the public affairs department balances off one set of opinions with another. I really do not think this is an unreasonable stricture to place upon the responsible authorities. For this reason I rise now to say, with respect, that the minister appeared in her answer to be tilting at windmills which do not exist. I take my stand in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to change the metaphor just used by the hon. member for Winnipeg South. A few weeks ago the minister ran up a brave set of colours on the ship of broadcasting. It disturbed me this afternoon to see those colours run down at the first wisp of semantic gunpowder.
The problem, and the minister knows it, is that if subclause (d) is unamended by a further set of safeguards, it will become the Magna Carta of extremism. Forces wishing to present views held by few Canadians, if any,
January 24, 1968	COMMONS
will justify their actions by using subclause
(d)	and telling us they are taking advantage of the reasonable opportunity afforded for expressing conflicting views on matters of public controversy.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I think even the hon. member for York South would agree that some months ago there was no necessity for the C.B.C. to bring a neo-nazi all the way from Germany to appear on one of its programs. But having decided not to bring him to Canada, the C.B.C. televised an interview with him. There should have been some responsibility to see that a measure of expression was given to the more generally held view in Canada regarding that menace to democratic life.
Unamended this bill will become the bill of rights for biased broadcasting. If we can interpret what "reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views" means, it seems to me we can equally well interpret what the expression "broadly held opinions" means so that those in charge may be alert to them. The C.B.C. has been dramatically unresponsive to public outcry on matters of public controversy. I believe it important that this bill spell out means whereby the public of Canada can call their creation, the C.B.C., to account.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make one more comment in answer to the minister's remarks. After all the good lady has gone through during the last couple of years with regard to broadcasting and the C.B.C., it seems to me she should have more sympathy with the intent of this amendment. Management control of C.B.C. broadcasting during the past few years has not been satisfactory either to her or to the public. I do not know what she meant when she referred to rotten management, but if she was referring to the type of control management has had over programs then I agree it has been rotten management.
As has been mentioned, this legislation will become a bill of rights for both the public and the broadcasters. We are attempting to make it an adequate bill. It is our responsibility to put teeth and backbone in it in so far as we can legislate on these matters. I agree we cannot spell them out in detail, but I believe this amendment would strengthen the hand of management with respect to programming.
This amendment is a very legitimate and reasonable one. It is intended to do nothing
DEBATES	5919
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting more than strengthen the bill so far as management is concerned so that it will be able to provide the control which 1 was pleased to hear the hon. lady say she believed management must have over programming as well as over the technical and financial aspects of broadcasting. We are dealing with this bill in a nonpartisan manner, and again I urge members of the committee to support this amendment. In its present form the bill does not provide anything better than what we have had in the past so far as broadcasting is concerned. Unless we put a little more starch in the bill we will not have anything better than what we have had. It is with this intent that I appeal for support for the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I wish I had the felicity of language to say how much I oppose the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer. Sometimes it troubles me to think that the democratic fabric of this country cannot stand a little bit of abrasion once in a while. I do not always want to know what the broadly held views of the people of this country are. I think it is dangerous just to pay lip service to the most broadly held views. We should be hearing other views.
In my opinion it was a very good thing for this country-I am not talking about the mechanics of management because that is none of my business-to see the neo-nazi, von Thadden, and to have him exposed just as Rockwell was exposed. It brought back to memory the horror and the evil that were in the world in the decade prior to the second world war. Did the fabric of this country wither because von Thadden had a few minutes on the public broadcasting system? Of course it did not. We saw this man and the evil he represented. I do not want to hear only broadly held views. The broadly held views of this country have a thousand media, a thousand ways to be heard in newspapers, magazines and other publications. I think it is time that we heard other views in this country and I shudder to think of parliament exercising that type of control over our public media.
I am going to vote against this amendment. From his speech the other day I can only take it that the hon. member does not know what satire is. The other night the C.B.C. ran a little bit of satire on Noah, Moses and other interesting figures in the Old Testament. Can we not laugh any more in this country? It was amusing. Is our Christian belief to those who have it-there are many who do not
5920	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting have it-so fragile that we cannot talk about Noah and the ark? I think it must have been quite tough for Noah to spend all that time in the ark. That is all that young man was saying, but apparently the whole fabric of Christianity is supposed to have been placed in jeopardy in those few minutes. I think it is very dangerous for the public broadcasting system to have to spend all its time showing the broadly held opinions of Canadians. Those broadly held opinions have ample protection.
You did not feel that way when von Thadden was to appear.
I never said a word about von Thadden.

Mr. Chairman, I wish I had the verbal facility of the hon. member for Royal to express my feelings about the subject of public broadcasting. Time and time again in this chamber I have seen members rise to protest vehemently against certain types of programs which sometimes appear on our national broadcasting system, over it or through it, or however the programs are transmitted. But over the years it seems it has been impossible for the majority in this parliament, representing the majority of the Canadian people, to get it across to the people responsible for preparing programs that there is a certain type of program which is generally unacceptable to the people of this nation.
* (4:00 p.m.)
Some people like classical music, some like drama, some like public affairs programs. These are all good. Before I go further I would like to say that the C.B.C. has done a wonderful job in some respects and that I am all for the C.B.C. We in Canada need the C.B.C., but somewhere in the works there are producers who are able to put out programs which are unacceptable. In looking over the record it would seem that there are always some producers who keep on probing and probing the line of acceptability. Sometimes they are on the one side and sometimes on the other. Sometimes they go too far and sometimes they stay within the limits of acceptability. However, they seem to be forever probing that line, trying to get away with everything they can get away with.
I intend to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer. It may not completely cover the situation. It is very difficult to take care of a situation of this kind in a legislative way, but at least the

DEBATES	January 24, 1968
amendment is an attempt to put more teeth in our broadcasting rules and regulations for the sake of control and keeping within the limits of general public acceptability the programs which are put out over our national system.
We can be proud of our national system. It belongs to all the Canadian people. Because it is a public system we have a public image to uphold, the image of the Canadian government. Whenever these unacceptable programs are put on the air we tend to destroy the image of the government, the identity of Canada, the image of Canada. That is what we do when we put these unacceptable programs on the air. Anything that can be done to strengthen the hand of the C.B.C. management so that they can control and manage these apparently uncontrollable and unmanageable producers within the organization will be an improvement. The more strength we can put in the hands of the management of the C.B.C. the better.
I am glad, therefore, to support this amendment and any other amendment which will tend to strengthen the hand of management. The C.B.C. is a great institution. Let us maintain the honour and integrity of that institution.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to intervene briefly in this discussion because I think a fundamental difference in philosophy has been revealed between those who support this amendment and those who, like myself, oppose it. I believe we are entirely wrong in thinking it is useful to attempt by legislation to deal with matters of taste and judgment or the sort of thing the hon. member for Middlesex West had in mind when he said we should not allow anything which is generally unacceptable to be put over the public broadcasting system. Who is to decide what is generally unacceptable? I suggest that if we have producers with competence and a reasonably intelligent management we must give them freedom not to decide what is generally acceptable to the public but to decide whether what is being done lives up to competent technical standards and leaves some freedom for the creative ability of the people doing the job.
If the suggestion is that the C.B.C. is to exercise censorship over these people who have to do the job and say that something is unacceptable to the public, then I would ask, what does this mean? What may be generally acceptable to one section of the public may be generally unacceptable to other sections. What does the hon. member for Red Deer
January 24, 1968	COMMONS
mean when he says the commission, I suppose, must be alert and respond to public preferences in this and other aspects of public programming? Of course they will be responsive in a general way in considering what public preferences may be but, as the hon. member for Royal said, it will be a sorry day when we have to wait and try to find out what is conventional, what is generally acceptable and what is the public preference before we allow creative artists and people of that ilk to deal with these matters.
May I add that the adoption of these words would be an absolute waste of time and energy. We cannot legislate by adding words. It has been suggested that we should strengthen the hand of management in dealing with these matters. I suggest that we would be doing precisely the opposite by putting in words of this sort. It has been suggested that the C.B.C. should be given the responsibility for censorship, which no sensible management would want to exercise. I believe that the principles of true liberalism-and I use the word with a small "1"-include the philosophy of freedom of thought and expression. I suggest that this type of amendment is not only illiberal but, if it has any effect at all, is also restrictive and damaging to the system we are trying to protect.

Mr. Chairman, this discussion is gradually becoming a discussion on the basic right of free speech. Some of the speeches we have heard seem to be crusading speeches which go much farther than the intent of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer. As I look at the wording of the original clause I find that the only specific reference to any particular type of programming in subclause (d) of clause 2 is the following:
-should provide reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy-
I would say that without this specific reference to controversial matters the first few words of the subclause really cover everything that is required in the field of programming. It reads:
-the programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should be varied and comprehensive-
That covers everything. I assume that the hon. member for Red Deer and others who have supported the amendment, such as the hon. member for Winnipeg South and a few others who have spoken, object that the only
DEBATES	5921
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting specific reference is the statement that controversial matters should be considered. It goes without saying that if there is wide and varied programming everything is covered. Yet it is stressed that we should emphasize controversial matters. The crusaders for freedom have criticized the amendment which I believe is quite mild in form. The amendment makes specific reference to another aspect of public communication in the following words:
-while ensuring that the most broadly held opinions receive appropriate consideration-
In other words, if we refer specifically to ensuring that there shall be controversy we must make sure also that non-controversial matters shall be taken into consideration. I see some of my friends in the New Democratic party smiling. If we are going to mention specifically that there must be controversy, then there is just as much reason to mention in addition the fact that the broader opinions accepted by the Canadian public should also be given consideration. If we go on in this way we can make this clause as long as an arm and deal with all items of communication which might be mentioned.
In my opinion all we need in Canada is a good Hyde Park corner such as there is in London where a person can go on any evening of the week or on any Sunday and talk about anything under the sun without restriction. You can shout into the breeze to your heart's content. A similar place in New York is called Bug House square. We do not have a Hyde Park corner in Canada and neither do we have a Bug House square. As a result we have tended in the past to turn our national broadcasting system into a Hyde Park corner and we emphasize the controversial aspects without emphasizing those things which are part of public opinion and of the body politic in Canada. I think such an institution might well be established in Canada. There is no attack on freedom in the words of the amendments, any more than there is an attack on freedom when you emphasize controversial matters. I support the amendment.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a very brief observation in relation to the amendment which appears to me to reflect the fear of censorship about which we hear a great deal. It seems to suggest again our often expressed concern about protecting our misguided people.

Judge not lest ye be judged, Murdo.
5922	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting

I have discovered from past experience that very often people are not afraid that they will be corrupted but that someone else will be corrupted by these things if we do not censor them to keep other people from hearing or seeing them.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he not realize we are not talking about censorship but rather about a clear channel of responsibility?
Mr. Marlin (Timmins) Censorship by any name is still censorship so far as I am concerned. I think we might do well if we all stopped for a moment and thought about this situation. We already have censorship of television programs. I have yet to see a television set that does not have a switch to shut off the set if you do not like a program. Perhaps we should pass an amendment requiring the manufacturer to put an extra large button on each set or something to remind people that if they do not like a program they have a switch to turn the set off.
I do not believe I am better equipped than anyone else to judge what my fellow Canadians should or should not see. I think they are perfectly capable of making that decision for themselves. I hope they in turn feel I am capable of deciding which programs I want to watch. We tend to get carried away sometimes by our attitude of protection for our fellow Canadians. They are perfectly capable of protecting themselves and they have ample opportunity to do so at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I think the attitude which ought to have been taken by the hon. member for Greenwood when he spoke with some heat but not much light a little while ago should have been to strike out the whole clause. We have included in the bill under the general title of a broadcasting policy for Canada a clause which deals with programming. I have been told by people active in the television and radio fields that we should keep away from this area because there is such a variety of opinion in respect of programming. In any event the government has introduced this clause. For that reason it is important that members have something to say about it.
We start from the premise that there will be a wide variety of opinion as to what is suitable, interesting, desirable or undesirable. This is also true of ordinary theatrical productions as well as movies and art. What is agreeable to one person may be disagreeable to another. Having had this matter put before
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
DEBATES	January 24, 1968
us in respect of television we are entitled to express our opinions on programming. Unless we express those opinions there will be no guidance for those who are in charge; yet the government has proposed a guiding clause.
The government suggests that programming should be varied and comprehensive, that there should be an element of public controversy, or at least that it should not be avoided, and that it should be of high standard, using predominantly Canadian creative and other resources. Those are four guide lines for C.B.C. management. They are a bit reminiscent of the guide lines laid down by the Prime Minister for his cabinet colleagues a couple of years ago and similar to the type of guide lines he should now produce for the candidates for leadership of the Liberal party.
People need guidance and the government is now suggesting that the directorate of the C.B.C. should have some guidance with regard to programming because it is in the area of programming that troubles have occurred in the past. We would not have had the many discussions here or investigations by committees unless there had been some public discontent about the nature of certain C.B.C. programs. The C.B.C. got itself into a great deal of difficulty over the years by attempting to go too far.
When I do not like a program, and particularly if it is a speech by a member of the N.D.P., I turn the set off. The hon. member for Timmins can rest happy in that regard. I am not an ardent t.v. fan. I prefer to read a newspaper, a book or Hansard. Nevertheless, I do watch a certain amount and I am able to form an opinion on whether or not I like a program. The C.B.C. has got itself into needless difficulty because of carelessness in respect of programming. I have never phoned a T.V. station to object to a program, nor have I written a letter to a station or to the management of the C.B.C.
I have not spoken frequently in the house on this subject. However, I am invited to do so now because this bill directs our attention to programming. I want the directorate of the C.B.C. to know what the members of this house think about programming, in addition to what they will read in these four guide lines to which I have referred. If we are going to have guide lines as suggested here I see no reason for rejecting the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer or any other similar amendment. The directorate of the C.B.C. will then know precisely
January 24, 1968

what the members of parliament think about programming.
The amendment is directed to all broadcasting.

I am glad the hon. member mentioned that because it does relate to all broadcasting, private stations as well, and to anything in connection with broadcasting.
As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris so wisely asked, why draw particular attention to the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy? Why at this stage do we have to draw to the attention of broadcasters that this is what we think they should be doing? They have been doing this for years. Why do we specifically have to mention that, and who decides what is public controversy?
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
There are certain people within the broadcasting field who make these decisions in some smoke-filled room. Talk about politicians making decisions in smoked-filled rooms! This is done by a handful of people in the broadcasting business in some smoke-filled room. They ask, I am sure, "What will be the subject for our discussion on the program next Sunday night? Let us see. There is a mysterious drug that somebody on some island in the Pacific ocean has taken and has died from it. Let us give that information to the public so that some of the students in our universities will get their hands on this drug and try it out as well." That is the type of program to which I object. These decisions are made by a handful of people sitting in some smoke-filled room.
Dalton Camp?

They come to a decision as to some subject of public controversy that they would like to bring before the people. Then there are the other manipulators who say they want to waken us up. They want people to engage in discussion. They want to alert us to the facts of life. A lot of this is such arrant and silly nonsense. There are quite a number of people here who have had a fair amount of experience of all facets of life and we do not need any more exhilarating ideas with regard to what we should experiment with and what we should do.
Speak for yourself on that point.

There is a handfull of people somewhere deciding whether this would be
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting good. They say, "We will stir things up and then we will get letters, some objecting and some approving. We will count them up and see how many approve. If there are not enough people who approve, we will write to our friends and ask them to get a letter in quickly because we are on the short end of letters approving our program." I have been in politics long enough to know how some of these things are arranged.
I see no objection to the rather mild amendment moved by the hon. member. It has been years since I have been able to approve of anything put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer. Mellowing as the years pass by, like the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and becoming very positive in my statements, I would like to say that for once I approve of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer. I hope it will be incorporated in the guide lines for the directors of broadcasting so they will realize that in addition to matters of public controversy we would like some attention paid to opinions that are broadly held. We think that those opinions should also receive appropriate consideration. There is nothing wrong with that at all. If we must listen to opinions that are held by only a small segment of the population, can we not also have programs that will be viewed with interest by a broad section of the population? That is all this amendment is suggesting. Consequently, sir, I shall support the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief.
I merely want to say that our group wishes to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). It is an amendment which does not ask much, which is very simple, and which may mean a lot because it asks, for once in this house, to take into consideration the preferences of the general public and make an effort to give it a small service since it is the public that foots the bill.
I always considered the C.B.C. as an impenetrable place, in every sense, for serious people and those who want to keep a moral sense to their life. I think it is at the programming level that the difficulty arises. Some producers take advantage of television on the pretext that they have the right to express controversial ideas and, in fact, they express these ideas all year round to a population which wants sound programming, in keeping with its faith and its social condition.
5924	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
In fact, we are not in Africa, we are in Canada, in a democratic country and I believe it is time for the government, if it intends to act-and I am not sure that such is its intention-to clean up this stable of the C.B.C.
Too often, we find producers like Mr. Kea-ble on the program "Tirez au Clair" or others who, ever so often, present the best atheists, the best unbelievers and the best free-thinkers, when it is not homosexuals or lesbians. Those programs are presented and we have to look at them, because there is only one channel in our area.

Mr. Chairman, I say it is time to defend the general public whose business this is because, after all, they are footing the $100 million deficit that the C.B.C. accumulates, to poison, soil and corrupt our youth.
Mr. Chairman, I think that if the government wants to do something, the bill under consideration at the present time provides a unique opportunity. It is time

I have said it many times-to do a clean-up job at the C.B.C. relate to the discussion we have been having this afternoon. It has been a very interesting discussion. I for one am not one of those who believe that the broadcasting system which is operated in the public service is meant only to perpetuate ideas commonly and publicly held. When we deal with something as important to the lifeblood of the nation's mentality as the broadcasting system, it seems to me that what we should expect to receive from it from time to time are things which are disturbing to our minds and to our consciences. If we are not going to require that we receive such things from time to time from the broadcasting system, then we are simply paying for amplified mediocrity. I feel there is an element in the amendment as it is proposed that would merely preserve for all of us a kind of bland public opinion which would do little for the edification of the Canadian people generally. It would be sad to see the public broadcasting system descend to this kind of performance.
May I point out also that I believe there is an incipient or subtle anti-Canadianism in this amendment which disturbs me greatly. In the second part of the amendment, following the words "Canadian creative and other resources" it is suggested we add the words "While alert and responsive to public preferences in this and other aspects of programming". All of us in this chamber know, I think, that we have created, almost against the stream of public opinion, a broadcasting system in this country in order to preserve some kind of cultural identity in the great sea of communications and propaganda which washes over us on a regular hour by hour and day by day basis from the great nation to the south of us. If the subject and the content of broadcasting were left purely to the majority of public opinion we would have no effective Canadian broadcasting in this country, and we should face that fact. By supporting this kind of amendment we would be chipping away a little bit here and a little bit there at the concept of truly worth-while broadcasting in this country.
I for one do not plan to support the amendment. Hon. members have suggested in the debate this afternoon that freedom is not
January 24, 1968

being attacked in these two amendments. On the surface they seem to be rather innocuous and inoffensive, but I would remind hon. members that freedom is not usually destroyed by frontal attacks. I urge all hon. members on both sides of the house to realize that in supporting this kind of amendment we are supporting a very real reduction in the concept of freedom of speech as we have allowed it in our institutions.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. N. Thompson (Red Deer) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO AFFORD GREATER PROTECTION AGAINST ARBITRARY INTERFERENCE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to amending the provisions of the Expropriation Act (R.S.C. 1952, c. 106) with a view to giving greater protection to citizens against arbitrary interference with their property rights by departments of the federal government, and to the establishment of more suitable procedures for the transfer of title and possession of land expropriated under the authority of this Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the last few days several members of the house have asked me what prompted me to introduce this motion, as I have done for the past four years. May I refer to an incident that occurred in January of 1964 which resulted in my becoming personally familiar with the Expropriation Act now on the statute books. At that time the Department of National Defence had expropriated a quarter section of land from a farmer in my constituency for the purpose of constructing communication towers necessary for defence installations. The department moved in to acquire the land. The farmer protested; he did not think the settlement offered was fair. He did not wish to give up his land. As a result the department made an arrangement by which he

January 24, 1968
Expropriation Act
could continue to live on the land and pasture his cattle there. The men involved in the construction of the towers repeatedly left the gates open and as a result the cattle got out on to the road allowance. The farmer became angry and an unfortunate situation developed between him, his neighbours in the community where he lived, and the Department of National Defence. Finally the Department of National Defence decided to use the Expropriation Act to take over this land forcibly.
Early in January, 1964, while the house was in recess, I received an urgent message for help. I drove out some ten miles to this property to find that a carload of R.C.M.P. and two truckloads of army personnel were already there together with another truck to haul away personal effects and a stockliner to haul away the stock. The pigs had got out of the chute and soldiers were chasing them through the snowdrifts. The officer in charge had lost his composure and had given the soldiers orders to use axes on the walls of the house and demolish it to the extent that the farmer could no longer live in it. By the time I arrived an angry crowd of neighbours had gathered and we were on the verge of a war between them and the military personnel.
The action taken on this occasion was entirely contrary to provincial laws which do not permit a man to be evicted during the winter months. Further, it was entirely contrary to the expropriation legislation of the province of Alberta which through certain provisions in the provincial legislation protects the rights of individuals when the government finds it necessary to take over private property.
Government expropriation of private property is an unfortunate necessity in the planned development of our cities and towns, but the rules which govern expropriation should require that the needs of the property owner be weighed against the needs of the state. Not only must there be the assurance of fair compensation and adequate warning to property owners that their land is to be expropriated, but public hearings must be held before a judge to determine whether the action is necessary and is in the public interest. Justice demands that no citizen should be deprived of his property without such a hearing. Expropriation powers which permit the filing of a plan to take away the ownership of a man's land when his certificate of title tells him he is still the owner are the reason I have placed this resolution before the house urging that the government amend the Expropriation Act.

Abraham Lincoln once said that when individual rights and property rights conflict, the rights of the individual must be given first place. I believe this is an important statement. When I came back to Ottawa to investigate just what were the expropriation laws of the land which permitted the Department of National Defence to take the action it did against this farmer, I was amazed to find that practically everybody in the department as well as the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) and the former minister of justice were in agreement that the expropriation law should be amended to make it less severe. In fact, committees had been working to this effect for a number of years but seemingly they never reached the point at which their findings were incorporated into legislation and presented to the house.
As I interpret the Expropriation Act, the mere fact that we here in parliament pass an act approving the construction of any public work gives officers of the civil service down to quite junior level the right, by merely drawing up and filing a plan in the appropriate registry office, to deprive a citizen of the land he owns and upon which he lives, leaving him nothing except the right to go to a court to collect some money. There is no requirement to follow the usual provincial laws in connection with transfer of title. There is no requirement for a public hearing to find out whether the land is indeed needed for public purposes. In a nation which has placed the legislative fields of property and civil rights within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, the powers granted by this act seems to border on the unconstitutional.
It might indeed be reasonable that in time of war and imminent danger to this country the federal government should have such powers. It was during such times that the present law was passed by this house. In other words, this is emergency legislation, amended in the early years of the second world war and intended to meet the demands of that emergency. It has never been amended to suit peacetime needs and to protect the rights of individual Canadians.
Powers such as these do not belong in the Expropriation Act. They belong in the War Measures Act. We already have far too much punitive federal law on our statute books. I am thinking particularly now of the Income Tax Act and of some provisions of the Excise Tax Act which are justifiable enough in times of national emergency but are an open threat to the liberty and property of citizens now
January 24, 1968

that this country has been at peace for 20 or more years.
This act has been used as a club in the hands of the National Capital Commission. I have been much interested in a case between Ethel V. Grayson and the Queen in reference to which Chief Justice Thorson of the exchequer court had this to say:
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Under these provisions a man's land can be lawfully taken from him without his consent, and even without his knowledge or any notice to him, merely by the deposit of record in the proper land titles or land registry office of a duly signed plan and description of the land. This may be done whenever the minister of the department charged with the construction and maintenance of the public work for which the land is to be taken deems it advisable to do so. On such deposit the expropriation of the land is complete without any further act by anyone. Whatever right, title or interest the former owner, or any other person, had in or to the land is immediately extinguished and the land is automatically vested in Her Majesty the Queen free and clear of any claims to or encumbrances upon it. All that is left to the former owner of the land, or a person having had a claim to or an encumbrance upon it, is a claim to compensation, which by section 23 of the act is made to stand in the stead of the land. And I might add here that the settlement of claims to compensation is frequently unconscionably delayed.
I have frequently called attention to these provisions of the law and stated that Canada has the most arbitrary system of expropriation of land in the whole of the civilized world. I am not aware of any other country in the civilized world that exercises its right of eminent domain in the arbitrary manner that Canada does. And unfortunately, the example set by Canada has infected several of the Canadian provinces in which a similar system of expropriation has been adopted.
These words come from a man whose knowledge of the law is without question. He made this statement in one of the very few cases where an individual who had his land expropriated had the means to appeal to the only court available to him, the exchequer court. I know of one case of land expropriation by the National Capital Commission in which a man living within the confines of the metropolitan city of Ottawa took his case to the exchequer court but finally gave up after spending some $28,000 or $29,000 in the presentation of his case. Yet we call this justice. It is time we did something about it.
It is not good enough that we go on and on saying that this law is not the right kind of law and that we must revise it. We simply have not enacted legislation to amend it, to make it as just as it should be and as just as every citizen of our country expects it to be. I believe it would be very easy and proper to provide that before any land is taken for a
Expropriation Act
public purpose by expropriation, except in time of war, a public hearing should be held before a judge so that everyone can be satisfied that it is in the public interest for that land to be taken. No citizen, I believe, should ever be deprived of his property without at least having the privilege of his day in court.
Second, I believe the exact method of expropriation should be spelled out, such as a certain number of days' notice, and disclosure of the intent of the authority. In addition, a safeguard should be provided so that no land would be expropriated unnecessarily or by mistake. I can cite a number of cases of expropriation by the National Capital Commission where this actually was the case, but the land was never returned to the owners from whom it was expropriated after the N.C.C. did not carry out the purpose for which it stated it required the land at the time of expropriation.
I suggest that a clause be inserted elsewhere in the statutes of Canada guaranteeing Canadian citizens the right to own property and that this clause should be specifically quoted in the Expropriation Act. If we did this we would be protecting the rights of Canadian citizens as they deserve to be protected.
Again I say, referring to the words of wisdom passed on to us by Abraham Lincoln, that when individual rights and property rights are in question the right of the individual must be given first place. Mr. Speaker, the expropriation laws of this country do not give the individual citizen first place. Consequently it is high time the government amended those laws in such a way that the rights of the individual Canadian citizen to property ownership are respected and guaranteed.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO AFFORD GREATER PROTECTION AGAINST ARBITRARY INTERFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the mover of this motion. He has brought up a most important subject. However, I do not agree with all his remarks and conclusions.
The entire matter of expropriation was brought forcibly to my attention in December, 1965, when the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority expropriated approximately 4,000 acres in the Welland area for a Welland canal bypass. This was a major land acquisition and affected the welfare of approximately 330 families. The impact on my riding was far reaching and most dramatic. It made me aware of possible injustices and possible inadequacies in our existing expropriation laws.
5S32

January 24, 1968
Expropriation Act
My remarks are neither in defence nor criticism of the present government. Our federal expropriation laws have been in existence for many years, under both Conservative and Liberal administrations, so there is no partisan blame to be assigned. I know that various governments have considered changes in these laws but, as often happens with this type of obscure legislation, with no aggressive lobby to promote changes lethargy sets in and no action is taken. However, I am happy to relate to the house that something is being done. The government is reviewing the entire situation with respect to expropriation and intends to bring in radical amendments to our expropriation laws. I do not believe this will be in this session. I hope it will be in the next session. This brings up a most important point.
The lack of review of many of our statutes indicates a real need for a continuing perusal of all our statutes to ensure their adequacy to meet changing times, conditions and circumstances. Therefore I advocate most strongly the establishment of a permanent law reform committee to appraise our statutes continually, including such ones as the federal Expropriation Act which was first enacted in 1886. This permanent committee could be comprised of government representatives, members from all parties in the house, and recognized experts in all broad fields of knowledge which affect the material and spiritual wellbeing of our citizens. It would be their duty to examine all existing statutes and make recommendations for change.
A prime example of this need was our divorce act. It had been in force for many years without change. It was entirely discordant with present codes of conduct, family views and marriage concepts. For years thousands of Canadians suffered under that antiquated and unjust act. Eventually the general opposition to it seeped through to parliamentarians and finally action was taken. A law reform committee could have made a study of that statute and made recommendations to the government in power perhaps years ago. In all probability the net result would have been the earlier rectification of the most unsatisfactory state of our divorce laws.
The reason I make these observations at this time is that the motion before the house, urging the government to consider changes in the law of expropriation, clearly indicates the necessity for a permanent type of law revision or reform committee to be given the

responsibility of continually reviewing our statutes.
As I have indicated, the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority expropriated 4,000 acres in the Welland area. Thus it can be seen that the whole question of expropriation is most important and far reaching. At the present time another gigantic expropriation is taking place in the St. Catharines area. Expropriations are being carried out all across Canada. More will follow. I agree with the mover of this motion that a change in the laws should be made as quickly and as efficiently as possible.
Let us take a brief glimpse at the history of expropriation. In our contemporary society property right is no longer the absolute right it used to be years ago, no matter what Abraham Lincoln said about it. Ownership of real estate is now subject to all kinds of regulations concerning town planning, zoning and construction bylaws. One of the most radical encroachments on private property rights is the power to expropriate. Expropriation in Canada is governed by statutory law, and some of the statutes provide for compensation and some do not.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
This is perhaps a revelation to members of the house. When dealing with existing expropriation legislation in Canada one starts off with the premise that expropriation is one case in modern life where public and private interests clash. The first important question in matters of expropriation is to find out who has the right to expropriate one's property and what this right is. The right to expropriate, being an unusual and far reaching right, must be found in the express words in the statute.
It should be observed that owing to Canada's federal constitution and the division of legislative powers between the federal and provincial governments there are two sets of expropriation laws, federal and provincial. The most important act so far as the federal government is concerned is the Expropriation Act. Under this act the minister of any federal government department charged with the construction and maintenance of any public work may take possession of any land, real property, water or stream which he judges to be necessary for the public welfare.
In addition to the Expropriation Act at least one dozen acts of parliament give expropriation powers to federal bodies including crown corporations. Some of these are the
January 24, 1968

Railway Act, the War Measures Act, the National Harbours Board Act, the Dominion Water Power Act and the Canadian Broadcasting Act. In the province of Ontario approximately 17 different acts include provisions by which the powers of expropriation can be exercised. It should be noted that expropriation proceedings are divided into two parts, the expropriation itself which results in the transfer of the owner's title to property to the expropriating body and the allocation of compensation for the land expropriated.
In practical terms-and I agree with the previous speaker-there is nothing one can do to oppose the principle of expropriation. There is no requirement that notice be given. Immediately the order is registered and title passes the expropriating authority can take possession. On the surface this would appear to be a most drastic and perhaps arbitrary procedure, but I think it should be given some consideration. I believe there is another side of the coin. If notice were given and there was a court hearing, in all probability-this has been the experience in the past-land speculators would buy up these properties. Fast sales would be made and when the actual expropriation took place the price of the land would be highly inflated. Although the idea of sudden expropriation perhaps has a traumatic effect on the owner involved, the purpose is to freeze the land values for one purpose, that the public, Canadian citizens, are not paying more for the land than they should.
Once the land is formally expropriated the next vexing question is how to arrive at the amount of compensation. In principle the compensation should place the owner in the same economic position he was in before the expropriation. Unfortunately, variations in the wording of different statutes have led the courts to apply somewhat different standards under different statutes for determining the compensation. Authorities on the matter all agree that there is a definite need for a uniform procedure in effecting expropriation, coupled with uniform compensation provisions.
The expropriating authority normally obtains an appraisal of the property. If through negotiation the two parties agree, that is the end of the matter. If there is disagreement the party which is the expropriating authority obtains another appraisal. If there is still disagreement the only recourse is to the exchequer court. So it can be seen that the expropriation procedure in
Expropriation Act
Canada is drastic and final but, if due consideration is given to it, I believe it will be apparent that perhaps in the general interest of the Canadian taxpayer this type of procedure is necessary.
The principles for determining compensation are most important to the parties concerned. Some of the various statutes which authorize expropriation do not even mention the means of arriving at the amount of compensation, but the general principles can be found in the leading cases. One salient point emerges. The amount to be paid is the value to the owner, not the value to the taker. It is also the value to the owner and not simply the market value. The first thing an expropriated owner should do, if there is any sign of disagreement about price, is to hire a competent appraiser. I bring out these points in order to refute the argument to the effect that the expropriated owner is helpless. The appraiser can give the owner an honest and unbiased appraisal of the property. This enables the owner to decide whether or not he should accept the offer. Later, if necessary, that appraiser can give evidence before the court.
When a market value has been obtained the total claim in a federal expropriation should normally be computed by adding to the best market value the special value to the owner, the interest from the date the owner goes out of possession, the usual 10 per cent compulsory taking allowance-this is an important point because it shows a reasonable attitude-and, where only part of the property has been taken, a claim for severance. The losses involved for the owner are also taken into account. These include, for example, the cost to move to another location, the cost of dismantling and reassembling machinery and equipment, the loss because of increased costs in the new location, and the cost of dislocation while moving. Compensation for expropriation of course must not be exorbitant because it must be remembered that the Canadian taxpayers must be protected against paying an exorbitant price for property.
The previous speaker mentioned his experience in expropriation matters. I should like to mention mine. From personal knowledge I feel that the extensive expropriations carried out in the Welland area by the seaway authority have been carried out with efficiency and tact. No doubt there have been isolated cases of injustice, but the seaway authority working under the existing law in my opinion has interpreted it fairly and liberally. Out of

January 24, 1968
Expropriation Act
331 expropriations only one may have to be decided by the court.
However, there is one aspect of this type of expropriation which bothers me. I know this has caused hardship in my area. This hardship results from the policy of taking the appraised value at the time of the expropriation and then not making the payment until months later. When the expropriated owner finally receives his money, based on a market value of a year previously, he finds that in the interval, because of the hundreds of buyers who have been competing for adjacent property, prices of properties in which he might be interested are inflated. When the expropriated owner looks for another property he finds in some cases that he must accept a property of lesser value than the one he left. In my opinion this is an injustice. I believe the government should investigate this aspect and make recommendations in this regard immediately.
I believe the expropriating body should treat each case individually. There is a splendid example of this in the Welland area. A family with 12 children had their property expropriated. They were living in a very comfortable home. It was suitable for them. However, when they received the expropriation money it was not sufficient to buy a home which would suit their needs. This is where extra effort and compensation are required. The seaway authority went to great lengths in finding a comfortable home for these people.
I believe that all expropriating authorities should hire appraisers not only for their competence but also for their compassion and their understanding of human nature. We must never forget that we are taking someone's home which has intangible values, and an individual's dignity and self-respect must always be the prime concern of an expropriating authority. I also believe, as the previous speaker mentioned, that there should be a more expeditious and summary procedure for expropriation. The existing system involves arbitration which is cumbersome, costly and slow.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Furthermore, if the expropriating authority wishes to take possession of a property before a final award is adjudicated then that authority should pay a substantial percentage of the appraised value. This is done by the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority which pays 80 per cent of the appraised value if a person wishes
[Mr. Tolmie.l
to leave his premises and property to locate elsewhere.
Very often the decision to expropriate is based upon preliminary surveys before the authority goes ahead with expropriation. If any damage is caused then the owner should be compensated. Provision should be included in our expropriation laws to grant assistance to certain categories of expropriated persons. For instance, an indemnity should be given to tenants with low incomes when the buildings they live in are expropriated, and the expropriating authority should also assist such families in their efforts to find other accommodation. Provisions should be explicitly placed in the expropriation laws to assist the resettlement of small tradespeople, craftsmen and small manufacturers. Again, there should be greater uniformity in the actual expropriation procedures and principles of compensation across Canada.
One proposal which seems to have merit is that relating to the drafting of a national code of expropriation which would set forth one uniform procedure. The anomalies and diversities resulting from too large a number of different laws dealing with expropriation would disappear if we had a uniform and equitable system of expropriation described clearly, simply and in a practical manner. Again I commend the hon. member for bringing this subject before the house. With the rapid and radical evolution of state ownership for public purposes the entire question of expropriation rights is in my opinion of transcendent importance.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO AFFORD GREATER PROTECTION AGAINST ARBITRARY INTERFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to thank the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane) for his courtesy in permitting me to precede him. I think he was ahead of me and had the right to speak first. I am very glad to be able to give enthusiastic support to the motion of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), and I commend him for bringing this urgent and important matter forward.
The present expropriation laws are a source of very serious injustice to quite a large number of people. We all know that expropriation is necessary because of expanding public and government needs. The public interest requires sometimes that private property rights give way. However, we have to recognize that there are highly emotional issues involved when people are asked, for the public benefit, to forgo property for which they may have worked and in which
January 24, 1968

they have deep feelings as well as their fortunes invested. The very fact that this parliament, among other legislative bodies, is constantly expanding the sphere in which expropriation takes place makes it all the more important that we should take our responsibility in seeing that there are not injustices in this field.
I want to commend to the attention of the house only two or three points in respect of the motion and the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer. The first is the point he made that there should be some sort of a review by a tribunal and a public hearing before land is actually taken. When a public authority or department decides it requires lands it should inform the person whose property will be taken and he should have the right to a public hearing to ascertain whether that land or property is reasonably necessary for the purpose for which it is sought. A hearing of this sort would make a tremendous difference and a provision of this kind should be included in expropriation procedures.
The other main difficulty that arises relates to the question of compensation. This is a very difficult matter because we live in a complex age in which values are constantly shifting. This is not an easy matter to determine. The plain fact is that the balance is not even as between the state and the individual. The state or the public authority is armed with plenty of money, experience and expert advisers both in the legal and valuation fields. The individual often feels helpless because he has not the means to hire the necessary people if a balance of justice is to be found. Any procedures which are brought about must take account of that factor to make sure that the individual whose property is expropriated has the means of obtaining the proper expert advice in the valuation and legal fields. Without it he has no genuine bargaining power and cannot expect or hope to get complete justice. This is tremendously important because there are only a few individuals who have the means or the desire to litigate a matter in the exchequer court or other courts. I imagine that in nearly all cases there is a settlement long before they reach the courts, but a settlement will not be fair if the expropriating authority has all the power, knowledge and bargaining experience and the individual has none.
As the last speaker suggested, I believe that parliament should be foremost in setting up model legislation in this field. I suppose
Expropriation Act
that our Expropriation Act and the Exchequer Court Act as well, because it comes into this, are as antiquated pieces of legislation as will be found in Canada. The province of Ontario and other provinces have moved toward a more satisfactory expropriation procedure. Even these are not satisfactory. The law reform committee of the province of Ontario has recommended further important changes.
I promised my hon. friend to be brief and I will live up to that promise by saying, with all the force I can command, to the government or any of its representatives who are here and paying attention to this debate that what the hon. member for Red Deer has suggested should have very high priority in the legislative program of the government. It should have high priority because it is not good that this parliament should be responsible for the right to interfere with the property and the lives of individual Canadians when the remedies of those Canadians are, by reason of the deficiencies of the legislation passed by this parliament, of such a nature they do not provide them with a fair chance to meet the problems with which they are suddenly faced.
I do not think we can underestimate the importance of this matter because justice is involved as well as the deep feelings of a great number of our citizens. I am not always in agreement with the hon. member for Red Deer but in this instance I think his motion is timely and deserves the greatest support possible.
