speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to commend the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) for bringing the subject of expropriation before the house. I thank the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) for his assistance in promoting changes in the acts relating to expropriation. I was very pleased to hear the fine address of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie), although I must say it will be very difficult for me to match his eloquence. His remarks were very understandable and much to the point.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Since the hon. member for Red Deer told the house how he became so very interested in the matter of expropriation, perhaps I should say a word or two about how I became so interested. My interest is not of so great a vintage as his. As hon. members know, during this session I have addressed

January 24, 1968
Expropriation Act
the house on this subject on October 4 and November 21.
The reason I became interested in expropriation was that Canadian National Railways decided to build a spur line 12J miles in length through the Fort Saskatchewan settlement in my constituency to a government subsidized Imperial Oil fertilizer plant just south of the town of Redwater.
Canadian National Railways notified 23 farmers, without having given any previous warning, that a portion of the land on their farms had been expropriated and registered in the land titles office. This was before they received any notification that the spur line was to go through their farms. This is a most unfair and, to my mind, very wrong way to conduct this type of business. I fully realize that there are cases where summary action must be taken to expropriate land, but in this case I think it was done in a most unfair and undemocratic way.
This is not the only case in which I am interested. As I remarked on November 21 last, as reported at page 4541 of Hansard, a few days after I had made my first address I was telephoned by a lady in Toronto whose home, a solid brick house, had been expropriated by the city of Toronto. No settlement had been made and her house was just destroyed. This lady's land was not going to be put to any good use, but that is what happened. This matter has not been settled. The authorities eventually offered her $10,000 for property that could have been sold for somewhere around $30,000, and she had to go to court. I do not know what the result has been.
There are many other cases of this type of thing. I have been informed of similar cases in the city of Edmonton and in other parts of Canada where farmland has been most summarily expropriated without the people concerned being given any opportunity to make arrangements ahead of time. I believe this is not right and is not in accordance with our democratic principles in this country.
We have on the statute books of Canada the Bill of Rights which ensures certain civil rights to the people of this country. The Bill of Rights provides as follows:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,
(a) the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property,
[Mr. Fane.J
and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;
I very freely admit that chapter 106 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, which covers the Expropriation Act, gives certain people the right to expropriate private property. However, I think that the owner of the property should have the right and the privilege not to have his land or property expropriated until he has refused to deal with the department that wants to take over certain of his property for improvement.
Section 3 of the Expropriation Act gives the minister of whatever department is concerned the power to enter into and upon any land to whomsoever belonging, survey and take levels of the same, and make such borings, or sink such trial pits as he deems necessary for any purpose relative to the public work. This section of the act goes on for another half page. I do not have the time at my disposal to read into the record all the things the section provides.
It is high time that we in this country who are so proud of our nation, who are so proud of our democratic principles and civil rights, made it mandatory that a person affected by the act be consulted and given an opportunity to make an agreement with those who want his land. This should be done before any expropriation is effected. After land is expropriated the only recourse that an owner has, if he is not satisfied with the settlement offered, is to appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
In almost every case brought before the Exchequer Court of Canada there is a minimum cost of about $20,000. Most people who have had their land expropriated do not have that kind of money to spend in an attempt to save property that is being taken away from them. I believe that of necessity these cases have to be heard in Ottawa, but it is a very expensive matter for people from my part of the country, for instance, to come here and have their case tried before the exchequer court. The $20,000 I mentioned does not cover the payment of the legal representatives of the people who are making the appeal.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I think that in cases like this the onus of proving the right to expropriate the property should be on the federal government or the government concerned, and the costs of the appeal to the exchequer court should be borne by the federal government and not by the person whose property is expropriated. It should be absolutely mandatory that the civil
January 24, 1968

rights provided in the Bill of Rights and in most of the laws of our country be adhered to. A person should not have to suffer the expropriation of his property in a manner which, in the cases to which I referred at the beginning of my remarks, practically amounts to theft because it was not necessary for Canadian National Railways to build a spur line from Fort Saskatchewan to Redwater through some of the best farming land in Canada and to cut up these farms in the way they did. The C.N.R. did not honour the commitments which were made on its behalf to build underpasses for the passage of stock when the line was built. Also the C.N.R. did not construct proper crossings over the railway line.
I believe that a time limit should be set when final settlement must take place. I know of cases where litigation has continued for years and no settlement has been reached. I definitely believe that the government should bear the cost of appeals to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
This is all I have to say on this subject. Again I wish to commend the hon. member for Red Deer for bringing this matter before the house and I thank you, Mr. Chairman, for allowing me the opportunity to make my comments.
